Findora is a digital lost-and-found ecosystem designed to simplify, accelerate, and secure the process of reporting, identifying, and recovering lost personal belongings within communities, academic institutions, and public venues. Traditional lost-and-found mechanisms often suffer from fragmentation, lack of secure verification, high friction in communication, and inadequate tracking. Findora addresses these shortcomings through a centralized web and mobile architecture featuring real-time feed updates, multi-criteria categorization, automated matching algorithms, and a multi-step ownership verification protocol.

APPENDIX: PROJECT FORMATTING AND SUBMISSION GUIDELINES

In modern urban, academic, and commercial environments, misplaced and lost belongings represent a frequent and distressing occurrence. Every day, thousands of individuals lose critical personal items such as wallets, national identification cards, academic documents, electronics, keys, and personal accessories. Despite advancements in consumer technologies, traditional methods for recovering lost items remain largely manual, fragmented, and inefficient. Community boards, social media groups, and physical lost-and-found desks suffer from limited reach, lack of verification mechanisms, and high communication overhead.

Findora is conceived as an integrated, community-driven web and mobile platform engineered to bridge the gap between finders and seekers. By leveraging structured reporting, automated matching criteria, secure item claim workflows, and reward/reputation scoring, Findora establishes a trustworthy digital infrastructure that transforms lost item recovery into an efficient, transparent, and collaborative process.
The primary objective of the Findora project is to engineer and deploy an end-to-end lost-and-found management ecosystem. The specific goals include:
To develop a responsive web portal and Android mobile application for instant reporting of lost and found items.
To implement an automated matching engine that pairs newly reported lost items with reported found items based on category, date, location, and visual descriptors.
To establish a secure, multi-stage claim verification mechanism requiring claimants to provide specific proof-of-ownership answers before sensitive contact details are revealed.
To incorporate a community reputation and reward system that incentivizes honest reporting and speedy returns.
To deliver a comprehensive administrator moderation dashboard for monitoring listings, preventing fraudulent submissions, and managing system security.

The purpose of Findora is to eliminate the friction and vulnerability inherent in traditional lost item retrieval. By providing a centralized digital repository with verified user identities and structured claim verification, the platform minimizes the risks of fraudulent claims and facilitates the rapid reunion of owners with their lost belongings.

The scope of this project encompasses the design, implementation, and evaluation of the core Findora ecosystem, including: User registration and JWT-based authentication; CRUD operations for Lost and Found item listings with rich media uploads; category-based search and filter queries; automated claim initiation and approval protocols; an in-app notification pipeline; and a backend administrative dashboard powered by Django REST Framework and PostgreSQL.

Findora is engineered for universal deployment across diverse community settings, including college and university campuses, airports, transit hubs, shopping complexes, conference venues, and municipal districts. Its modular API architecture allows easy customization and integration into third-party organizational intranets.

The development of Findora achieved several crucial software engineering milestones: seamless cross-platform integration between a Python Django backend and native Android/web clients; strict validation of image and location metadata; robust role-based access control safeguarding user privacy; and sub-second query performance for multi-criteria item lookups.

This project report is systematically structured into seven comprehensive chapters: Chapter 1 introduces the project background, goals, and scope; Chapter 2 surveys existing academic literature and commercial solutions; Chapter 3 delivers detailed requirements analysis, specifications, and conceptual models; Chapter 4 presents the

architectural, database, and UI design; Chapter 5 outlines the implementation details, coding practices, and testing strategies; Chapter 6 showcases experimental results, app snapshots, and user documentation; and Chapter 7 concludes the report with reflections on achievements, limitations, and future enhancements.

Research in human-computer interaction and community software systems demonstrates that prompt item recovery depends critically on two factors: visibility of information and trust in the return channel. Studies on community behavior indicate that finders are generally willing to return valuable items if the process is simple, secure, and preserves personal privacy. Furthermore, contemporary web frameworks and microservice architectures offer unprecedented capabilities for real-time spatial indexing and automated similarity matching.

A comparative review of existing solutions—such as Facebook Lost and Found Groups, physical university helpdesks, and general classified portals (e.g., Craigslist)—reveals significant limitations. Social media groups lack structured metadata fields and search indexing, leading to post clutter. Physical desks are restricted by operating hours and geographic boundaries. Commercial classifieds do not offer proof-of-ownership verification, exposing users to scams.

Chapter 4 detailed the end-to-end structural foundation of Findora. The multi-tiered architecture and normalized relational schema ensure scalability, security, and consistent transactional throughput across all client interactions.

Findora’s backend was implemented using Python and Django REST Framework, leveraging Django’s Model-View-Template (MVT) architecture decoupled into REST API endpoints. The client applications interact with the server via JSON payloads over HTTPS. Token authentication is maintained through secure SimpleJWT access and refresh tokens.

Code modularity was enforced through dedicated Django apps for accounts, items, claims, notifications, and analytics. Data access queries were optimized using Django ORM's select_related and prefetch_related methods to prevent N+1 query bottlenecks.

To achieve optimal server performance, file uploads undergo automated compression and resizing before storage. Database indexes were added to frequently queried columns (category, status, created_at) to ensure rapid search indexation.
A multi-level testing methodology was executed to guarantee software reliability, fault tolerance, and security.
Unit tests were written using Django’s test runner (APITestCase) covering user authentication, model validation rules, claim status transitions, and permission enforcement.
Integration tests validated end-to-end workflows: user registration -> item creation -> search query -> claim filing -> claim acceptance -> reputation point incrementation.
A beta deployment was distributed to a cohort of 30 college students and faculty members. Feedback was gathered on usability, response time, and clarity of verification prompts.

Based on beta feedback, several enhancements were incorporated: streamlined image cropping, in-app push notifications on claim updates, and automated email alerts when potential item matches are detected.

6.3 Operational Workflow and Comprehensive User Guidelines

Findora provides a unified, step-by-step workflow designed to streamline lost item recovery while eliminating fraud and maintaining complete transactional accountability. The end-to-end operational lifecycle spans eight primary phases:

1. User Registration & Security Onboarding: New users create a verified account with legal name, contact credentials, and avatar. Session tokens are securely cached for seamless app launches using EncryptedSharedPreferences and JWT tokens.

2. Reporting Lost Belongings: Owners document missing items by selecting category, entering distinct descriptive identifiers, setting loss date/time, providing location context, and uploading optional reference photos.
3. Posting Discovered Property: Finders photograph discovered items, specify the discovery location/time, and define a secret verification question that only the rightful owner can accurately answer.
4. Automated Matching & Community Discovery: The platform indexes active reports in real time, notifying owners when a matching found item is logged within the same spatial-temporal proximity.
5. Secure Ownership Claim Submission: Claimants review item details and submit private answers to the secret question along with optional evidence (purchase receipts or serial numbers).
6. 1-on-1 End-to-End Encrypted Coordination: Finders and owners communicate via real-time in-app chat to coordinate a safe public handover location without sharing private phone numbers.

7. Dual-Confirmation Handshake & Reputation Rating: Upon physical item return, both parties click 'Confirm Return'. The system marks the item resolved, awards community reputation points, and collects finder star ratings.
8. Administrative Oversight & Moderation: Platform moderators review flagged posts, audit disputed claims, verify proof documents, and manage community trust scores via the web admin console.

Findora successfully solves the communication and verification gap in lost and found management. By establishing an organized, secure, and reward-driven digital platform, Findora empowers communities to recover lost belongings swiftly while safeguarding user privacy.

The system's significance lies in its automated matching engine, secure claim validation, and community reputation incentives. Unlike chaotic social media channels, Findora provides structured accountability and verifiable records for every reported item.

Current limitations include reliance on user truthfulness for verification question evaluation, dependency on active internet connectivity, and the absence of computer-vision-based automatic image matching.

Future enhancements will incorporate: AI-powered image similarity matching using convolutional neural networks (CNNs); geolocation-based real-time proximity alerts using Geofencing; integration with campus smart card RFID readers; and automated SMS gateway notifications.
